.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:9:AI assistants across all CLI runtimes (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini) consistently defaulted to Grep and Glob for code search even when CocoIndex (semantic search) and Code Graph (structural queries) were available and better suited. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:27:**Problem:** Hardcoded routing rules would cause confusion when a tool was unavailable. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:29:**Fix:** Each enforcement layer checks whether CocoIndex and Code Graph are actually available before recommending them. If CocoIndex is down, the server instructions and PrimePackage omit the semantic search rule entirely. If the Code Graph is empty, structural query routing is excluded. The AI receives only actionable recommendations for tools that are actually running.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:41:**Fix:** Added a "Tool Routing" section to `buildServerInstructions()` in `context-server.ts` containing three conditional rules: CocoIndex for semantic/concept searches (only included when CocoIndex is available), Code Graph for structural queries like callers and dependencies (only when graph is fresh or stale), and Grep for exact text or regex (always included). .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:45:**Problem:** The PrimePackage (the structured context payload sent on the first tool call of a session) told the AI what tools existed but not when to use each one. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:47:**Fix:** Extended the `PrimePackage` interface in `memory-surface.ts` with a `toolRouting` field inside `routingRules`. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-025-tool-routing-enforcement.md:53:**Fix:** Added code-search pattern detection in the tool dispatch handler. When `memory_search` or `memory_context` is called with a query matching code-search patterns (phrases like "find code", "implementation of", "function that", "where is", "how does X work"), the JSON response envelope gains a `hints` array suggesting CocoIndex or Code Graph instead. Hints are non-blocking -- they append to the response without interrupting the current tool call, nudging the AI toward the right tool on the next query.

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-011-compaction-working-set.md:9:When an AI session runs long and the context window fills up, Claude compacts the conversation to free space. Previously, that compaction only preserved memories -- it had no awareness of which code files were actively being worked on or what the codebase structure looked like. This phase replaces the Memory-only compaction with a three-source merge pipeline that combines constitutional memory, structural code graph context, and semantic code search results. A new session working-set tracker remembers which files and symbols were touched during the conversation, so when compaction fires, the system knows what matters most and allocates its limited 4000-token budget across all three sources using guaranteed minimums, overflow redistribution, and a deterministic trim order that protects the most critical context.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-011-compaction-working-set.md:21:**Fix:** Built a late-fusion pipeline that retrieves from three independent sources in parallel: (1) constitutional and triggered memories from the memory database, (2) structural code graph context showing file relationships and dependencies, and (3) CocoIndex semantic search results finding conceptually related code. The three result sets are deduplicated at the file level (so the same file mentioned by two sources only appears once, keeping the higher-priority version) and merged into a single structured brief. "Late fusion" means each source runs its own retrieval independently -- they are only combined at the end, which avoids ordering dependencies and lets each source use its own timeout. After compaction, the AI now retains awareness of active code files, their structural neighbors, and project-wide rules.

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-020-query-routing-integration.md:9:When a user asked a question about their codebase, they had to know which tool to call: `code_graph_context` for structural questions ("who calls this function?") and `memory_search` for semantic ones ("find code similar to X"). .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-020-query-routing-integration.md:23:**Fix:** A classification step called `classifyQueryIntent()` was added at the top of the `memory_context` handler. Users simply ask their question in plain language and the system determines where to look.

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-016-cross-runtime-ux.md:31:**Problem:** The system offers two search backends: the code graph (which understands structural relationships like "what calls this function" or "what does this class extend") and CocoIndex (which understands meaning, like "find code similar to this pattern"). .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/changelog/changelog-024-016-cross-runtime-ux.md:33:**Fix:** A new heuristic classifier called `classifyQueryIntent()` examines query keywords before routing. When the query is ambiguous -- no clear signal either way -- it runs against both backends so results are not missed. This removes the guesswork of which search tool to invoke for a given question.

PrimePackage is a post-selection correction mechanism, not a pre-selection router. The live PreCompact-style compaction path is currently an in-band MCP pre-dispatch hook, not an implemented external Claude hook script. The runtime chain starts at `context-server.ts` `CallToolRequestSchema`, checks whether the incoming call is `memory_context` with `mode === 'resume'`, extracts a context hint, and routes that hint through `autoSurfaceAtCompaction(contextHint)` before the tool handler runs. `autoSurfaceAtCompaction()` only trims/validates the string and delegates to `autoSurfaceMemories(sessionContext.trim(), 4000, 'compaction')`. `autoSurfaceMemories()` then calls `getConstitutionalMemories()`, `triggerMatcher.matchTriggerPhrases(contextHint, 5)`, enriches constitutional hits with retrieval directives, and finally passes the assembled payload through `enforceAutoSurfaceTokenBudget(...)`. The returned value is either `null` or an `AutoSurfaceResult` object; nothing in this chain writes cache files or produces human-readable hook text by itself. The current repo does not yet contain the external `PreCompact` and `SessionStart(source=compact)` hook scripts described by the packet; those paths are still spec-level design. Phase 2 refines the same SessionStart-side behavior into a shared `session-prime.ts` that reads pending compact state, outputs cached context for `source=compact`, and falls back to `memory_context({ mode: "resume", profile: "resume" })` for resume-style recovery. There is also an important packet-level mismatch: Phase 1's fallback text omits `profile: "resume"`, but DR-007 and Phase 2 say every resume path must pass it. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/025-tool-routing-enforcement/research/iterations/iteration-003.md:2:## Focus: Analyze query classification patterns that distinguish semantic discovery (CocoIndex), structural navigation (Code Graph), and exact-text/path lookup (Grep/Glob), then design a lightweight routing classifier.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/025-tool-routing-enforcement/research/iterations/iteration-003.md:5:1. The MCP server already contains a lightweight structural-vs-semantic classifier, but it is only a 3-state `structural | semantic | hybrid` heuristic and is currently used inside `memory_context`, not as a universal first-tool router. `classifyQueryIntent()` scores keyword hits at 1x, regex-pattern hits at 2x, and picks a dominant class only when one side exceeds 65% of the total score; otherwise it falls back to `hybrid`. `memory_context` then uses that result to optionally attach code-graph context for `structural` or `hybrid` queries, while `semantic` or low-confidence queries simply fall through to the existing semantic path. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:1:# Iteration 051: Incremental Index Coordination — CocoIndex + Code Graph Sync
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:5:Determine how our planned structural code graph index should coordinate with the already-deployed CocoIndex semantic index so both stay useful without creating a brittle shared-refresh system. This pass focuses on change detection, watcher strategy, freshness exposure, branch-switch behavior, rebuild cost, and the smallest safe MVP coordination model.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:9:1. CocoIndex should be treated as an independently managed semantic index whose freshness is refreshed through its own daemon and command surfaces, not as a watcher we control directly.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:11:   The local CocoIndex docs are explicit about what is public: `ccc index` performs incremental updates on subsequent runs, `ccc search --refresh` forces a refresh before search, and the MCP `search` tool defaults `refresh_index` to `true`. The same docs also describe a daemon that auto-starts, continues background indexing after client disconnect, and serves search over IPC. What the docs do not document is a public "shared file watcher" contract, a Git-status-based detector, or a stable event stream we should subscribe to. That means the safest implementation assumption is: CocoIndex internally decides how to notice or reconcile file changes, while our integration should rely only on the supported refresh surfaces (`ccc index`, CLI `--refresh`, MCP `refresh_index`) and its reported status/freshness metadata. [SOURCE: `.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/references/tool_reference.md:80-104`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/references/tool_reference.md:203-247`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/SKILL.md:265-306`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/SKILL.md:372-377`]
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:13:   Inference: because the daemon exists and indexing can continue after client disconnect, CocoIndex likely has its own internal scheduling and refresh logic. But the packet evidence does not prove a repo-local file watcher API, so our design should not depend on one.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:21:   Our packet already states that graph-specific incremental updates remain independent of CocoIndex, and the CocoIndex docs describe a daemonized background system with its own concurrency caveats around repeated `refresh_index=true` requests. A shared watcher would create coupling at the least stable seam: event delivery, debounce timing, error propagation, and branch-switch recovery. It also risks turning one indexer's outage into a shared outage. The cleaner design is: each index owns its own refresh cadence, but both publish comparable freshness records that a higher-level orchestration layer can inspect. [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/research.md:472-487`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/decision-record.md:94-105`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/SKILL.md:372-377`]
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:27:   The packet's API research already recommends that stale graph data should still be returned when useful, but with explicit freshness metadata and warnings, while repair happens in the background or on scoped demand. That same pattern should apply to the combined system. If CocoIndex is fresher than the graph, semantic recall can still seed candidate files while structural expansion is marked stale or partial. If the graph is fresher than CocoIndex, structural neighborhood answers can still be served, but semantic similarity should be marked stale and potentially trigger a CocoIndex refresh on the next semantic query. [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-044.md:75-125`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-044.md:266-277`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-044.md:309-332`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-045.md:201-205`]

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:41:   Our packet already frames CocoIndex and the code graph as complementary but independent systems: "what resembles what" versus "what connects to what." That separation argues against a tightly coupled event bus or a single transaction boundary. The graph research also converged on background-first indexing plus scoped repair when stale, which maps naturally to a coordination layer that compares timestamps, pending jobs, and stale flags before deciding whether to use cached results, request a scoped repair, or warn. [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/decision-record.md:94-105`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/research.md:246-263`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-044.md:266-277`] [SOURCE: `.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-045.md:209-209`]

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:52:   CocoIndex's own skill guidance says to suggest reindexing after branch switches, major refactors, or large merges. The code graph packet independently classifies branch switches, pulls/merges, dependency changes, and grammar/schema changes as broader async rebuild triggers rather than per-save hot-path events. That suggests the coordination rule: on branch switch, both systems mark their freshness as suspect, run reconciliation, and only escalate to full rebuild when the delta is large enough or the index format changed. For the code graph that means scanning changed/deleted/renamed files and using content hashes and invalidation classes; for CocoIndex it means invoking its normal incremental rebuild path rather than assuming a watcher remained valid across checkout. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-051.md:56:   The CocoIndex docs say first indexing typically takes 1-5 minutes and later runs are incremental. Its pipeline includes scanning, chunk splitting, embedding generation, and vector storage, which is inherently heavier than syntax parsing alone and may also involve remote embedding APIs. By contrast, the code graph's hot path is expected to be "parse one file, extract local symbols/edges, update SQLite," and iteration 041 argues the parser itself is unlikely to be the dominant cost; downstream invalidation and dependency propagation matter more. Iteration 038 adds the strongest concrete Tree-sitter benchmark in the packet: parsing a 2,157-line Rust file in 6.48 ms, with incremental updates generally under 1 ms. That does not make the whole graph free, but it does support the cost ranking: full CocoIndex rebuild > full graph rebuild > graph scoped update. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:1:# Iteration 59: CocoIndex Utilization Improvements (Q16)
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:4:Investigate how CocoIndex utilization can be improved across four dimensions: (1) automatic re-indexing triggers, (2) smarter seed resolution in seed-resolver.ts, (3) query routing between structural (code graph) and semantic (CocoIndex) search, and (4) hybrid query patterns combining both systems for better results.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:12:**A. Fuzzy line matching is absent.** The exact match (`start_line = ?`) fails when CocoIndex chunk boundaries don't align perfectly with symbol start lines. CocoIndex's RecursiveSplitter uses 1000-char chunks with 150-char overlap, so chunk start lines often land mid-function rather than at the function declaration. A range-overlap query (`WHERE start_line <= ? AND end_line >= ?`) already exists as the "enclosing" fallback, but it's only tried after exact fails. A better approach: combine exact + near-exact (within N lines) before falling through to enclosing.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:21:This would match when CocoIndex reports line 45 but the function starts at line 43. Confidence: 0.95 (between exact's 1.0 and enclosing's 0.7).
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:29:**C. No score propagation from CocoIndex.** `resolveCocoIndexSeed()` discards the CocoIndex similarity score entirely -- it converts to a bare `CodeGraphSeed` and delegates. The original CocoIndex score could inform the confidence value of the `ArtifactRef`, especially when combined with resolution quality. A seed with CocoIndex score 0.9 + enclosing resolution should have higher confidence than one with CocoIndex score 0.3 + enclosing resolution.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:35:Currently, CocoIndex re-indexing is fully manual (`ccc index` CLI or `ccc_reindex` MCP tool). The daemon architecture supports background indexing, but no automatic triggers exist. Three trigger points are viable:
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:37:**A. On branch switch (git checkout/switch).** Branch switches are the highest-impact change event because they can modify hundreds of files at once. Detection approach: watch for `.git/HEAD` changes via file watcher, or intercept `git` commands via shell hooks. CocoIndex already handles file-level diffing during indexing, so a branch-switch trigger just needs to invoke `ccc index` (incremental). The code graph (`code_graph_scan`) already has incremental indexing via content hash -- coordinating both is the key challenge.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:39:**B. On session start.** The CocoIndex SKILL.md already mandates "ALWAYS check index status before searching" and "suggest reindexing if codebase has changed significantly." This could be automated: during SessionStart hook (or equivalent), check `ccc status` and auto-trigger `ccc index` if stale. The daemon's auto-restart on version mismatch shows this pattern already exists partially.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:41:**C. On file save (debounced).** Individual file saves are low-impact but frequent. A debounced trigger (e.g., 30 seconds after last save) would keep both indexes fresh. The code graph's `code_graph_scan` already supports incremental indexing with content hash checks, making individual file updates cheap. CocoIndex's daemon architecture supports background indexing and "search during indexing" (streams IndexWaitingNotice), so freshness wouldn't block searches.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:50:**A. Keyword-based pre-classification.** The CocoIndex SKILL.md already has intent signals with weighted scoring (SEARCH: weight 4, INDEX: weight 4, etc.). This pattern can be generalized to route between CocoIndex semantic search and code graph structural queries:
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:55:| "find code that does X", "implementations of" | CocoIndex (search) | Semantic/intent query |
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:57:| "how is X implemented" | Both (CocoIndex -> Code Graph) | Start semantic, expand structural |
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:60:**B. Confidence-based fallback routing.** When CocoIndex returns low-similarity results (all below 0.3), automatically fall back to code graph structural search. When code graph returns file_anchor resolution (no symbol match), suggest CocoIndex semantic search for better results.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:67:### 4. Hybrid Query Patterns: CocoIndex Seeds into Code Graph Expansion
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:69:The current architecture already supports CocoIndex -> Code Graph bridging via `CocoIndexSeed` type in seed-resolver.ts. But the pattern is one-directional. Three hybrid patterns would improve results:
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:71:**A. Structural expansion of semantic results.** After CocoIndex finds semantically relevant code, automatically expand via code graph to include callers, callees, and imported modules. This is already supported via `code_graph_context` with `queryMode: 'neighborhood'`, but the AI must explicitly chain the calls. An integrated `hybrid_search` tool could automate: CocoIndex search -> resolve seeds -> expand neighborhood -> merge into single response.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:73:**B. Semantic enrichment of structural results.** After code graph returns a call chain or dependency tree, use CocoIndex to find semantically similar code that isn't structurally connected. Example: after finding all callers of `resolveSeed()`, CocoIndex could find other resolution/lookup patterns in the codebase that use similar logic but aren't in the call graph.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:75:**C. Working set warm-up.** On session start, use the code graph to identify the "hot" files from the last session (files with recent edits tracked via `code_files.indexed_at`), then use CocoIndex to pre-fetch semantically adjacent code. This creates a broader initial context than either system alone.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:78:[SOURCE: /Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Opencode Env/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/lib/code-graph/seed-resolver.ts:18-25 (CocoIndexSeed type)]
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:80:### 5. Underutilized CocoIndex Features
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:82:Analysis of the CocoIndex MCP skill reveals several capabilities not fully leveraged by the current integration:
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:84:**A. Language and path filters are not passed through.** The CocoIndex `search` tool accepts `languages` (list) and `paths` (list) filter parameters, but the seed-resolver and code-graph-context modules don't pass these through when initiating CocoIndex searches. Using code graph file metadata (language column in `code_nodes`) to auto-filter CocoIndex searches by relevant language would improve precision.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:86:**B. `refresh_index` parameter management.** The skill documents a known concurrency issue: simultaneous `refresh_index=true` requests cause `ComponentContext` errors. The integration should track whether a refresh has occurred in the current session and automatically set `refresh_index=false` for subsequent calls. The `computeFreshness()` function in code-graph-context.ts already tracks staleness -- this could be extended to CocoIndex freshness.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:88:**C. `ccc_feedback` tool is available but never called.** The Spec Kit Memory MCP exposes `ccc_feedback` for submitting search result quality feedback, but no code path automatically calls it. After the AI uses a CocoIndex result (e.g., reads the file, uses the finding), implicit positive feedback could be logged. This would build a quality signal over time.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:95:- **Real-time file watcher for CocoIndex re-indexing**: Too complex for the current architecture. The daemon already handles background indexing; adding another file watcher creates duplicate infrastructure and coordination complexity. Debounced session-level triggers are sufficient.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-059.md:115:- What worked and why: Direct file analysis of both seed-resolver.ts and code-graph-context.ts alongside the CocoIndex SKILL.md revealed concrete improvement opportunities that wouldn't be visible from external documentation alone. The code shows exact gaps (missing near-exact matching, discarded CocoIndex scores, no auto-filter passthrough).

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/011-compaction-working-set/implementation-summary.md:70:The compaction pipeline now merges three sources (constitutional/triggered memory, structural code graph, CocoIndex semantic neighbors) through a budget-aware allocator instead of the previous Memory-only path. A session working-set tracker seeds graph expansion and semantic search at compaction time.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/011-compaction-working-set/implementation-summary.md:74:`working-set-tracker.ts` maintains a per-session record of files and symbols accessed during the conversation. Each entry tracks access count and last-access timestamp. `getTopRoots(n)` returns the top-N entries weighted by recency and frequency, used to seed `code_graph_context(queryMode: 'neighborhood')` and CocoIndex semantic queries at compaction time. Symbol-level tracking is supported via `trackSymbol()`.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/011-compaction-working-set/implementation-summary.md:78:`budget-allocator.ts` accepts a total token budget (default 4000, also supports 1500/2500) and per-source payload sizes. Floor allocations are enforced: constitutional 700, graph 1200, CocoIndex 900, triggered 400, overflow pool 800. When a source returns empty or under its floor, the unused tokens flow to the overflow pool and are redistributed to the highest-priority sources that can use more. When the total exceeds budget, a deterministic trim order is applied: semantic tail first, then graph leaves, triggered memories, direct neighbors, state/next-steps, and constitutional last (never dropped). Returns an `AllocationResult` with per-source granted budgets, dropped item counts, and redistribution metadata.

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/research.md:556:CocoIndex covering semantic search means the code graph can be **purely structural** and much simpler. No embeddings, no chunking, no vector search in the code graph at all. It becomes a lightweight relationship index that answers "what connects to what" while CocoIndex answers "what resembles what." The two complement each other without overlap.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/research.md:560:**Bridge Design** (iter 046): `code_graph_context` accepts file-range seeds directly from CocoIndex. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/research.md:562:**Chunk Alignment** (iter 047): CocoIndex uses structure-aware character chunking (~1000 chars), not true AST function-level splitting. Seed-to-node resolution: exact symbol → enclosing symbol → file anchor.

.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/010-cocoindex-bridge-context/implementation-summary.md:70:Phase 010 delivers the LLM-oriented orchestration layer that bridges CocoIndex semantic search results into structural graph neighborhoods. The `code_graph_context` tool accepts seeds from any provider (CocoIndex MCP, manual, graph), resolves them to graph nodes, expands structurally via Phase 009 queries, and returns compact context packages optimized for AI consumption.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/010-cocoindex-bridge-context/implementation-summary.md:74:The seed resolver normalizes three seed types (CocoIndex, Manual, Graph) into a unified `ArtifactRef` representation. CocoIndex seeds use `file` plus `range.start/end`, manual seeds resolve by `symbolName`, and graph seeds resolve by `symbolId`. Each seed follows a resolution chain: exact symbol overlap, near-exact symbol match within ±5 start lines, enclosing symbol, or raw file anchor. Every resolution carries a confidence score reflecting match quality. Overlapping seeds that resolve to the same graph node are deduplicated before expansion.
.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/010-cocoindex-bridge-context/implementation-summary.md:111:Implemented in plan order: seed-resolver first (foundation), then the context orchestrator with all three query modes, then server integration. .opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/024-compact-code-graph/research/iterations/iteration-037.md:161:Earlier packet research already established that tree-sitter, aider-style repo maps, and CocoIndex are relevant building blocks. This iteration adds a broader research-layer synthesis that was not previously captured: a clear taxonomy of code graph types, a task-to-graph suitability map, a comparison of graph richness versus construction cost, an industry comparison across CodeQL/Semgrep/Sourcegraph, and a direct recommendation about which graph projections are compact enough for LLM consumption. The most important new conclusion is that the right design is not "full code property graph in prompt," but "rich graph in storage, compact graph projection for the model."

.opencode/commands/memory/search.md:858:> **Note:** The dedicated `spec_kit_memory_memory_context()` tool provides unified intent-aware retrieval server-side. It accepts `input`, `mode`, `intent`, `specFolder`, governed retrieval params (`tenantId`, `userId`, `agentId`), `limit`, `sessionId`, `enableDedup`, `includeContent`, `includeTrace`, `tokenUsage`, and `anchors`. `spec_kit_memory_memory_quick_search()` also supports governed retrieval via `tenantId`, `userId`, and `agentId`. This is the recommended unified approach. The manual orchestration below is for advanced use cases requiring fine-grained control.
.opencode/commands/memory/search.md:860:> **Adaptive Fusion, Hybrid Routing & Telemetry:** Retrieval combines vector, FTS5/BM25, and graph channels, then applies intent-adaptive fusion and reranking. Results may be routed through artifact-class classification before scoring. When `SPECKIT_ADAPTIVE_FUSION` is enabled, weights adapt dynamically by intent, including the internal continuity profile (`0.52 / 0.18 / 0.07 / 0.23`) used for resume-style retrieval. When `SPECKIT_EXTENDED_TELEMETRY` is enabled, extended telemetry is captured (query timing, score distributions, fusion decisions) and written to the telemetry log, while `getRerankerStatus()` reports reranker latency and cache `hits` / `misses` / `staleHits` / `evictions`.

.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/SKILL.md:321:> **Fork-specific telemetry (skill bundles a soft-fork at `0.2.3+spec-kit-fork.0.2.0`).** Result rows carry seven additional fields that vanilla upstream cocoindex-code does NOT emit: `source_realpath` and `content_hash` (canonical chunk identity), `path_class` (taxonomy: implementation / tests / docs / spec_research / generated / vendor), `dedupedAliases` and `uniqueResultCount` (mirror-folder dedup signals), `raw_score` (pre-rerank score, preserved for audit), and `rankingSignals` (per-result rerank breakdown). Implementation-intent queries get a bounded `±0.05` rerank toward `path_class == implementation`. Full schema, types, examples, and reading guidance live in [`references/tool_reference.md` §7 Fork-Specific Output Telemetry](references/tool_reference.md#-7-fork-specific-output-telemetry); the canonical field-to-REQ mapping lives in [`changelog/CHANGELOG.md`](changelog/CHANGELOG.md).

.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:61:CocoIndex Code is a semantic code search tool built on vector embeddings. Where `grep` matches exact characters, CocoIndex Code matches meaning. Ask for "retry logic with exponential backoff" and it returns code that implements that pattern, regardless of how the author named variables or functions. This makes it the right tool when you know what a piece of code does but not where it lives or what it is called.
.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:63:The skill ships with two access modes. The CLI (`ccc`) is fastest for one-off queries and all index management operations. The MCP server (`ccc mcp`) exposes a single `search` tool that AI agents call directly via stdio transport, integrating semantic search into any tool-calling workflow without leaving the conversation.

.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:158:CocoIndex Code resolves queries by embedding the natural-language query text and comparing the resulting vector against pre-computed vectors for every code chunk in the index. This means the search engine reads intent, not characters. A query for "graceful shutdown handler" finds code that tears down servers or releases resources, even if the words "graceful", "shutdown", or "handler" never appear in that code.
.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:164:The CLI and MCP interfaces are complementary, not redundant. The CLI handles index management operations (`index`, `status`, `reset`, `init`, `daemon`) that have no MCP equivalents. The MCP server exposes only the `search` tool because index management is a human-initiated operation, not an agent-initiated one. When building an AI workflow that needs semantic search, configure the MCP server and let agents call `search` directly.

.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:496:A: Index management operations (`index`, `status`, `reset`, `init`, `daemon`) are intended for human-initiated workflows, not agent-initiated ones. An agent asking to reset a codebase index would be a destructive action with no confirmation step. The MCP interface exposes only `search` to keep agent behavior predictable and safe. Run index management commands from a terminal.
.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/README.md:502:A: Use Voyage Code 3 when search quality matters more than avoiding an API dependency. The local model (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) is a general-purpose sentence embedding model with 384 dimensions. It works well for most queries but can miss nuanced code patterns. Voyage Code 3 was trained on code and produces 1024-dimensional vectors, giving it better discrimination between semantically similar but functionally different patterns. Switch to it when you notice too many false positives or misses on important queries. Remember: switching models requires `ccc reset && ccc index`.

This avoids forcing one search system to handle both structural relationships and semantic similarity.

.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:276:**Tool-level TTL cache** remembers recent results for 60 seconds. When you save, update or delete a spec-doc record, the cache for affected searches clears automatically. You never see stale results.

.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:405:**Causal trust display badges** -- `memory_search` results carry an additive `trustBadges` payload per `MemoryResultEnvelope`, derived at response time from existing causal-edge columns. The `formatSearchResults()` formatter at `mcp_server/formatters/search-results.ts` batch-reads connected causal-edge data and attaches the following display-only fields to each result envelope: `confidence` (clamped from the strongest connected edge `strength`), `extractionAge` (human-readable age from the newest connected `extracted_at`), `lastAccessAge` (human-readable age from the newest connected `last_accessed`), `orphan` (`true` when the result has no incoming causal edges), and `weightHistoryChanged` (`true` when any connected edge has a `weight_history` row). The formatter fails open when the DB handle or `weight_history` table is unavailable, and preserves any precomputed `trustBadges` payload a caller already supplied. `mcp_server/lib/response/profile-formatters.ts` extends response-profile result typing so the `quick`, `research`, and `resume` profiles preserve the badge payload on `results[]` and `topResult` rather than dropping it during shaping. The placement decision is per-result, not top-level — the trust signal belongs beside the specific spec-doc record claim the user is judging. No schema change, no new relation types, no new storage of code/process/tool facts.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:448:**Session deduplication** -- pushes down results you already saw. If you got a result 3 turns ago, new searches rank it lower. Saves approximately 50% of tokens on follow-up queries.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:464:The system also learns from how you use search results:
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:472:**Mode-aware response profiles** -- formats results differently by situation. Quick lookup returns top answer only. Research returns full results with evidence. Resume returns state plus next-steps. Debug returns the full retrieval trace.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:474:**Empty result recovery** -- diagnoses why a search came back empty (too narrow filter, unclear question, missing knowledge) and suggests next steps.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:480:Beyond the core search pipeline, several enhancements make retrieval smarter at finding what you actually need.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:484:**Spec folder hierarchy search** -- uses your project folder organization as a retrieval signal. If you are looking at a child folder, the system also checks parent and sibling folders for related information.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:490:**Memory summary search channel** -- creates a short summary of each spec-doc record when saved and searches against those summaries. Like reading the back-cover blurb of a book.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:494:**ANCHOR-based section retrieval** -- indexed packet docs and generated continuity artifacts can include `<!-- ANCHOR:name -->` markers. The search system indexes individual sections separately, allowing retrieval of just "decisions" or "next-steps" from a large document (~93% token savings). Files above 50K characters are always chunk-split.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:508:**Embedding retry orchestrator** -- when the embedding service is temporarily unavailable, the spec-doc record is saved without a vector and queued for retry. A background worker retries until it succeeds. A temporary outage never permanently blocks full searchability.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:510:**Lexical-only fallback indexing** -- saves memories in a simpler text-searchable form when the embedding service is down. Keyword search still works. When the service returns, the system upgrades to full vector searchability automatically.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:514:**Chunked-save finalization** -- chunked saves track the created parent and child IDs so finalization stays transactional. Prediction-error supersede finalization records cross-path `supersedes` edges and marks predecessors superseded inside one transaction. Safe-swap updates null old-child `parent_id` values before bulk delete inside that same finalization step, and any finalize failure triggers compensating cleanup that removes the staged replacement chunk tree. Parent BM25 mutation is delayed until at least one chunk succeeds and, for safe-swap updates, until finalization completes, which preserves the old parent BM25 state when all chunks fail.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:516:**Dynamic server instructions** -- at startup, tells the calling AI how many memories are stored, how many folders exist and which search methods are available.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:522:Research-grade infrastructure for measuring and improving search quality over time.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:524:**12-metric core computation** -- grades every query across twelve quality dimensions (MRR@1/3/10, NDCG@10, MAP and more). Together they pinpoint exactly where search is struggling, like a doctor running multiple tests instead of just asking "do you feel sick?"
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:528:**Ablation study framework** -- turns off each search channel one at a time and measures quality degradation (Recall@20 delta). Identifies which components are critical.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:542:**Architecture:** CocoIndex (semantic, external MCP) finds code by concept. Code Graph (structural, this server) maps imports, calls and hierarchy. Memory (session, this server) preserves decisions. The compact-merger combines all three under a 4000-token budget for compaction injection. Code-graph source is self-contained under `code-graph/` with `handlers/`, `lib/`, `tools/`, and `tests/`.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:552:**Edge explanation and blast-radius uplift:** Edge metadata writes include graph-local `reason` and `step` JSON fields next to the existing `confidence`, `detectorProvenance`, and `evidenceClass` payload. `code_graph_query` relationship rows surface those fields for each edge, and `code_graph_context` propagates them through both structured edges and compact text briefs. `blast_radius` keeps the prior file-oriented payload while adding `depthGroups`, `riskLevel` (graph-local: `high` on ambiguity or depth-one fanout >10, `medium` on 4-10, `low` otherwise), an optional `minConfidence` traversal filter, `ambiguityCandidates`, and a structured `failureFallback` so callers never receive a bare error string when resolution cannot continue. The `code_edges` schema stays at `metadata TEXT` — the new fields ride inside the existing JSON blob.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:556:**Read-path readiness:** `ensureCodeGraphReady()` runs automatically inside `code_graph_query` and `code_graph_context`. It checks graph freshness, returns a `readiness` block, and performs bounded inline selective reindex only when the stale set is small enough to repair safely on the read path. Empty graphs, large stale sets, and other full-scan cases remain explicit `code_graph_scan` work.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:564:**CALLS disambiguation:** `code_graph_query` CALLS mode prefers callable implementation nodes over wrapper-shadow candidates for ambiguous subjects (e.g. `handle*`), and records ambiguity / selected-candidate metadata alongside the results so callers can audit the choice.
.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/README.md:566:**Query routing:** Structural queries (callers, imports, dependencies) go to `code_graph_query`. Semantic and concept queries go to CocoIndex (`mcp__cocoindex_code__search`). Session and memory queries go to `memory_context`.

   140	function toHybridResult(result: FusionResult): HybridSearchResult {
   141	  const sourceCandidate = (result as { source?: unknown }).source;
   142	  const primarySource = result.sources[0] ?? 'hybrid';
   143	  const scoreCandidate = (result as { score?: unknown }).score;
   144	
   145	  return {
   146	    ...result,
   147	    id: result.id,
   148	    score: typeof scoreCandidate === 'number' ? scoreCandidate : result.rrfScore,
   149	    source: typeof sourceCandidate === 'string' ? sourceCandidate : primarySource,
   150	  };
   151	}

    15	
    16	# Search Pipeline - 4-Stage Retrieval
    17	
    18	A four-stage retrieval pipeline that takes a search query through candidate generation, score fusion, reranking and final filtering to produce ranked memory results.
    19	
    20	---
    21	
    22	## Table of Contents
    23	
    24	- [1. OVERVIEW](#1-overview)
    25	- [2. STRUCTURE](#2-structure)
    26	- [3. PIPELINE STAGES](#3-pipeline-stages)
    27	- [4. KEY INVARIANTS](#4-key-invariants)
    28	- [5. RELATED DOCUMENTS](#5-related-documents)
    29	
    30	---
    31	
    32	## 1. OVERVIEW
    33	
    34	The `pipeline/` directory implements the core retrieval pipeline behind `memory_search`. Each search request flows through four sequential stages, each with a defined I/O contract and clear responsibility boundary. The pipeline supports hybrid, vector and multi-concept search types with optional deep-mode query expansion, cross-encoder reranking, MMR diversity pruning and MPAB chunk-to-parent reassembly.
    35	
    36	Gate E alignment: pipeline ranking is not the source of continuity truth. Resume-oriented callers should anchor on `/spec_kit:resume` and the `handover.md -> _memory.continuity -> spec docs` chain before using pipeline-ranked evidence.
    37	
    38	The public API is a single function: `executePipeline(config)` exported from `index.ts`.
    39	
    40	---
    41	
    42	## 2. STRUCTURE
    43	
    44	| File | Description |
    45	|------|-------------|
    46	| `index.ts` | Public barrel export. Re-exports `executePipeline` from the orchestrator and all pipeline type definitions from `types.ts`. |
    47	| `orchestrator.ts` | Wires the four stages together in sequence. Passes each stage's output as input to the next and assembles the final `PipelineResult` with per-stage metadata. |
    48	| `stage1-candidate-gen.ts` | Stage 1: Candidate Generation. Runs search channels (hybrid, vector, multi-concept), applies deep-mode query expansion (R6), embedding-based expansion (R12), summary embeddings (R8), constitutional memory injection, quality threshold filtering and tier/contextType filtering. |
    49	| `stage2-fusion.ts` | Stage 2: Fusion + Signal Integration. The single authoritative scoring point. Applies 9 signal steps in fixed order: session boost, causal boost, co-activation spreading, community co-retrieval, graph signals, FSRS testing effect, intent weights (non-hybrid only, G2 prevention), artifact routing, feedback signals, artifact limiting, anchor metadata and validation metadata scoring. |
    50	| `stage3-rerank.ts` | Stage 3: Rerank + Aggregate. Applies cross-encoder reranking (remote or local GGUF), MMR diversity pruning and MPAB chunk collapse with parent document reassembly from the database. |
    51	| `stage4-filter.ts` | Stage 4: Filter + Annotate. Removes results below minimum memory state priority, enforces per-tier limits, runs TRM evidence-gap detection and attaches annotation metadata. Enforces the score immutability invariant at runtime. |
    52	| `types.ts` | All pipeline data contracts: `PipelineRow`, `Stage4ReadonlyRow`, `PipelineConfig`, stage I/O interfaces (`Stage1Input`/`Output` through `Stage4Input`/`Output`), `PipelineResult`, `ScoreSnapshot` and the `resolveEffectiveScore()` shared score resolution function. Also provides `captureScoreSnapshot()` and `verifyScoreInvariant()` for Stage 4 defence-in-depth. |
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## 3. PIPELINE STAGES
    57	
    58	```text
    59	Query + Config
    60	      |
    61	      v
    62	  Stage 1: Candidate Generation
    63	      |  search channels, constitutional injection, quality filter
    64	      v
    65	  Stage 2: Fusion + Signal Integration
    66	      |  session/causal/co-activation boosts, intent weights,
    67	      |  artifact routing, feedback signals, FSRS write-back
    68	      v
    69	  Stage 3: Rerank + Aggregate
    70	      |  cross-encoder reranking, MMR diversity, MPAB chunk collapse
    71	      v
    72	  Stage 4: Filter + Annotate
    73	      |  state filter, per-tier limits, TRM evidence gap, annotations
    74	      v
    75	  PipelineResult { results, metadata, annotations, trace }
    76	```
    77	
    78	**Stage 1 - Candidate Generation** (`stage1-candidate-gen.ts`)
    79	- Runs one or more search channels based on `searchType` and `mode`.
    80	- Channels: hybrid (with optional deep-mode expansion), vector, multi-concept.
    81	- Optional R12 embedding expansion and R8 summary embedding channels.
    82	- Injects constitutional memories when absent and no tier filter is active.
    83	- Applies quality threshold and tier/contextType filters.
    84	
    85	**Stage 2 - Fusion + Signal Integration** (`stage2-fusion.ts`)
    86	- The only stage where scoring modifications happen (except Stage 3 reranking).
    87	- 9 signal steps applied in a fixed order that must not be reordered.
    88	- G2 prevention: intent weights are applied only for non-hybrid search types.
    89	- FSRS testing effect fires only when `trackAccess` is explicitly true.
    90	
    91	**Stage 3 - Rerank + Aggregate** (`stage3-rerank.ts`)
    92	- Cross-encoder reranking via remote API or local GGUF model.
    93	- MMR diversity pruning using per-intent lambda values.
    94	- MPAB chunk collapse: groups chunks by parent, elects best chunk, reassembles parent content from the database.
    95	- Preserves Stage 2 scores as `stage2Score` for auditability.
    96	
    97	**Stage 4 - Filter + Annotate** (`stage4-filter.ts`)
    98	- Memory state priority filtering, with the coldest retained-history rows treated as fallback evidence only.
    99	- Per-tier hard limits prevent any single tier from dominating results.
   100	- TRM evidence-gap detection (Z-score confidence check on score distribution).
   101	- Runtime score invariant verification via snapshot comparison.
   102	
   103	---
   104	
   105	## 4. KEY INVARIANTS
   106	
   107	1. **Single Scoring Point.** All score modifications happen in Stage 2 (fusion) or Stage 3 (reranking). Stage 4 must not change any score field.
   108	2. **G2 Double-Weighting Guard.** Intent weights are applied only for non-hybrid search types. Hybrid search incorporates intent weighting during RRF/RSF fusion internally.
   109	3. **Stage 4 Score Immutability.** Enforced at compile time via `Stage4ReadonlyRow` readonly fields and at runtime via `captureScoreSnapshot()` / `verifyScoreInvariant()`.
   110	4. **Score Resolution Consistency.** All stages use the shared `resolveEffectiveScore()` function from `types.ts` with fallback chain: `intentAdjustedScore` > `rrfScore` > `score` > `similarity/100`, clamped to [0, 1].
   111	
   112	---
   113	
   114	## 5. RELATED DOCUMENTS
   115	
   116	- `mcp_server/lib/search/` - Parent search directory containing hybrid search, vector index, cross-encoder and other search modules consumed by the pipeline.
   117	- `mcp_server/lib/ops/` - Background operations (file watcher, job queue) that feed data into the search index.
   118	- `@spec-kit/shared/contracts/retrieval-trace.ts` - Trace contract used for pipeline observability.
   119	- `@spec-kit/shared/algorithms/mmr-reranker.ts` - MMR algorithm used by Stage 3.

   129	/** Fetch full memory records required for FSRS tier classification. */
   130	function fetchMemoryRecords(memoryIds: number[]): Map<number, TierInput> {
   131	  const records = new Map<number, TierInput>();
   132	  if (memoryIds.length === 0) return records;
   133	
   134	  const db = attentionDecay.getDb();
   135	  if (!db) return records;
   136	
   137	  try {
   138	    const stmt = db.prepare(
   139	      'SELECT * FROM memory_index WHERE id = ?'
   140	    );
   141	    for (const id of memoryIds) {
   142	      const row = stmt.get(id) as TierInput | undefined;
   143	      if (row) {
   144	        records.set(row.id as number, row);
   145	      }
   146	    }
   147	  } catch (err: unknown) {
   148	    const message = toErrorMessage(err);
   149	    console.warn('[memory_match_triggers] Failed to fetch memory records:', message);
   150	  }
   151	
   152	  return records;
   153	}

   155	/** Get tiered content for a memory based on its tier state (HOT=full, WARM=summary, COLD=excluded) */
   156	async function getTieredContent(
   157	  memoryInfo: { filePath: string; title: string | null; triggerPhrases: string[] },
   158	  tier: string
   159	): Promise<string> {
   160	  if (tier === 'COLD' || tier === 'DORMANT' || tier === 'ARCHIVED') return '';
   161	  try {
   162	    const fs = await import('fs');
   163	    const validatedPath = validateTieredFilePath(memoryInfo.filePath);
   164	    const canonicalPath = validateTieredFilePath(fs.realpathSync(validatedPath));
   165	    const content = fs.readFileSync(canonicalPath, 'utf-8');
   166	    if (tier === 'HOT') return content;
   167	    // WARM tier returns truncated summary
   168	    return content.substring(0, 150) + (content.length > 150 ? '...' : '');
   169	  } catch (_error: unknown) {
   170	    console.warn('[memory-triggers] getTieredContent failed', {
   171	      filePath: memoryInfo.filePath, // server-side only; safe to log
   172	      tier,
   173	      error: _error instanceof Error ? _error.message : String(_error),
   174	    });
   175	    return '';
   176	  }
   177	}

    38	  source?: string;

    48	function shouldBlockReadPath(readiness: ReadyResult): boolean {
    49	  return readiness.action === 'full_scan' && readiness.inlineIndexPerformed !== true;
    50	}

    52	function resolveDeadlineMs(profile: ContextArgs['profile']): number {
    53	  switch (profile) {
    54	    case 'quick':
    55	      return 250;
    56	    case 'debug':
    57	      return 700;

    65	function resolveSeedSource(args: ContextHandlerArgs, anchor: {
    66	  filePath: string;
    67	  startLine: number;
    68	  endLine: number;
    69	  symbolId: string | null;
    70	  fqName: string | null;
    71	}): string | undefined {
    72	  const normalizedSeeds: NormalizedSeedSource[] = (args.seeds ?? []).map((seed) => ({
    73	    source: typeof seed.source === 'string' && seed.source.trim().length > 0
    74	      ? seed.source
    75	      : seed.provider,
    76	    filePath: seed.provider === 'cocoindex'
    77	      ? (seed.file ?? seed.filePath ?? '')
    78	      : (seed.filePath ?? seed.file ?? ''),
    79	    startLine: seed.provider === 'cocoindex' ? seed.range?.start : seed.startLine,
    80	    endLine: seed.provider === 'cocoindex' ? seed.range?.end : seed.endLine,
    81	    symbolId: seed.symbolId,
    82	    symbolName: seed.symbolName,
    83	  }));
    84	
    85	  const match = normalizedSeeds.find((seed) => {
    86	    if (seed.symbolId && anchor.symbolId) {
    87	      return seed.symbolId === anchor.symbolId;
    88	    }
    89	    if (seed.symbolName && anchor.fqName) {
    90	      return seed.symbolName === anchor.fqName || anchor.fqName.endsWith(`.${seed.symbolName}`);
    91	    }
    92	    if (seed.filePath !== anchor.filePath) {
    93	      return false;
    94	    }
    95	    if (typeof seed.startLine === 'number' && seed.startLine !== anchor.startLine) {
    96	      return false;
    97	    }
    98	    if (typeof seed.endLine === 'number' && seed.endLine !== anchor.endLine) {
    99	      return false;
   100	    }
   101	    return true;
   102	  });
   103	
   104	  return match?.source;
   105	}

   107	/** Handle code_graph_context tool call */
   108	export async function handleCodeGraphContext(args: ContextHandlerArgs): Promise<{ content: Array<{ type: string; text: string }> }> {
   109	  let readiness: ContextReadiness = {
   110	    freshness: 'empty' as const,
   111	    action: 'none' as const,
   112	    inlineIndexPerformed: false,
   113	    reason: 'readiness check not run',
   114	  };

   116	  try {
   117	    // Auto-trigger: ensure graph is fresh before querying

   119	      readiness = await ensureCodeGraphReady(process.cwd(), {
   120	        allowInlineIndex: true,
   121	        allowInlineFullScan: false,
   122	      });

   124	      // PR 4 / F71 step 5: surface as canonical 'error' freshness so
   125	      // buildReadinessBlock() maps it to canonicalReadiness='missing' +
   126	      // trustState='unavailable' automatically. Removes the manual
   127	      // trustState injection that previously lived at the response site.
   128	      readiness = {
   129	        freshness: 'error' as const,
   130	        action: 'none' as const,
   131	        inlineIndexPerformed: false,
   132	        reason: 'readiness_check_crashed',
   133	        error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err),
   134	      };
   135	    }
   136

   138	      const readinessBlock = buildReadinessBlock(readiness);
   139	      return {
   140	        content: [{
   141	          type: 'text',
   142	          text: JSON.stringify({
   143	            status: 'blocked',
   144	            message: `code_graph_full_scan_required: ${readiness.reason}`,
   145	            data: {
   146	              queryMode: args.queryMode ?? 'neighborhood',
   147	              blocked: true,
   148	              degraded: true,
   149	              graphAnswersOmitted: true,
   150	              requiredAction: 'code_graph_scan',
   151	              blockReason: 'full_scan_required',
   152	              readiness: readinessBlock,
   153	              canonicalReadiness: readinessBlock.canonicalReadiness,
   154	              trustState: readinessBlock.trustState,

    53	# Memory Search Command
    54	
    55	Unified entry point for knowledge retrieval and analysis. Combines intent-aware context search (retrieval mode) with epistemic measurement, causal graph tools, and evaluation dashboards (analysis mode).
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## 0. INSTRUCTIONS
    60	
    61	Start by classifying `$ARGUMENTS` into retrieval mode or analysis mode. Follow the routing contract below, prefer canonical packet sources in retrieval mode, and only invoke the analysis subcommands that match the user's explicit request.
    62	
    63	---
    64	
    65	```yaml
    66	role: Retrieval & Analysis Specialist
    67	purpose: Unified entry point combining intent-aware retrieval with epistemic measurement, causal graph, and evaluation tools
    68	action: Route through retrieval or analysis mode based on argument pattern
    69	
    70	operating_mode:
    71	  workflow: argument_routing
    72	  workflow_compliance: MANDATORY
    73	  approvals: none_required
    74	  tracking: intent_classification
    75	```
    76	
    77	---
    78	
    79	## 1. PURPOSE
    80	
    81	> **L1 Orchestration + L6 Analysis**: This command operates at both the L1 retrieval layer (orchestrating lower-level context-retrieval operations) and the L6 analysis layer (epistemic baselines, causal graph, evaluation). It provides a single entry point for all knowledge-related context-retrieval operations.
    82	
    83	Provide a unified entry point that:
    84	
    85	**Retrieval mode** (default):
    86	- Automatically detects task intent from the query
    87	- Applies task-specific weights for search optimization
    88	- Combines search + load in a single operation
    89	- Returns context with relevance explanation
    90	- Enforces L1 token budget constraints (target: ~2000 tokens per call)
    91	- Handles session deduplication for cross-session queries
    92	- Targets canonical packet sources first: `handover.md`, `_memory.continuity`, then the packet spec docs
    93	
    94	**Analysis mode** (subcommand-triggered):
    95	- Epistemic measurement: Capture knowledge baselines before and after tasks (`task_preflight`, `task_postflight`)
    96	- Causal graph: Trace decision lineage, create/remove causal links, view graph stats (`memory_drift_why`, `memory_causal_link`, `memory_causal_unlink`, `memory_causal_stats`)
    97	- Evaluation: Run channel ablation studies and view reporting dashboards (`eval_run_ablation`, `eval_reporting_dashboard`)
    98	- Learning history: View PREFLIGHT/POSTFLIGHT records and Learning Index trends (`memory_get_learning_history`)
    99	
   100	### Hybrid Retrieval Runtime (Retrieval Mode)
   101	
   102	The unified context tool runs a hybrid retrieval pipeline with **graph-first routing** (026):
   103	
   104	- **Graph channel has priority** in the fusion strategy: structural queries (callers, imports, dependencies) are routed to `code_graph_query` first, before semantic or lexical channels
   105	- Tri-channel retrieval (graph + vector/semantic + FTS5/BM25) with graph results given precedence in the fusion merge
   106	- CocoIndex semantic search (`mcp__cocoindex_code__search`) integrates as the vector/semantic channel, providing natural-language code discovery alongside indexed-continuity vector search
   107	- When graph and semantic channels miss or return weak results, a 3-tier FTS fallback activates: FTS5 full-text → BM25 keyword scoring → Grep/Glob filesystem search. Post-026 FTS5 remediation improved BM25 tokenization and ranking accuracy
   108	- Intent-adaptive fusion and reranking (weights adapt when `SPECKIT_ADAPTIVE_FUSION` is enabled, including the internal continuity profile: semantic `0.52`, keyword `0.18`, recency `0.07`, graph `0.23`)
   109	- MMR diversity pruning to reduce redundant chunks, with continuity-oriented Stage 3 passes using a dedicated lambda of `0.65`
   110	- Cross-encoder reranking only runs when at least 4 candidates reach Stage 3; `applyLengthPenalty` remains on the API surface for compatibility but currently resolves to a neutral `1.0` multiplier for every document
   111	- `getRerankerStatus()` exposes reranker latency plus cache `hits`, `misses`, `staleHits`, and `evictions`
   112	- Deep-mode query expansion for broader lexical coverage
   113	- Evidence-gap detection (026) to flag low-confidence retrievals with explicit gap warnings, enabling downstream reasoning to remain cautious and avoid acting on sparse evidence
   114	
   115	### Canonical Retrieval Order
   116	
   117	- `/spec_kit:resume` is the recovery surface for session continuation.
   118	- Resume-oriented retrieval follows `handover.md -> _memory.continuity -> spec docs`.
   119	- Packet-oriented retrieval may additionally use indexed `document_type='graph_metadata'` rows for dependency, supersession, related-packet, and key-file signals.
   120	- `find_spec` and `find_decision` should resolve against canonical spec docs and anchors, not against standalone continuity artifacts.
   121

   220	**Default fallback:** If no keywords match, defaults to `understand`.

     7	// Stage 1 is mandatory (throws on failure — no candidates = no results).

     9	// Timing is recorded for latency observability.
    10	//
    11	// I/O CONTRACT:
    12	// Input:  PipelineConfig (query, embedding, limits, flags, intent, session)
    13	// Output: PipelineResult { results: Stage4ReadonlyRow[], metadata, annotations, trace }
    14	// Key invariants:
    15	//     - results are scored by Stage 2, reranked by Stage 3, filtered by Stage 4
    16	//     - Score fields are frozen after Stage 3; Stage 4 output scores == Stage 3 output scores
    17	//     - Stage metadata for all four stages is included for observability
    18	//     - When a stage degrades, metadata.degraded = true and timing tracks each stage
    19	// Side effects:
    20	//     - Delegates to each stage; see individual stage modules for their side effects
    21	
    22	import type {
    23	  PipelineConfig,
    24	  PipelineResult,
    25	  Stage1Output,
    26	  Stage2Output,
    27	  Stage3Output,
    28	  Stage4Output,
    29	  Stage4ReadonlyRow,
    30	  SignalStatus,
    31	} from './types.js';
    32	
    33	import { executeStage1 } from './stage1-candidate-gen.js';
    34	import { executeStage2 } from './stage2-fusion.js';
    35	import { executeStage3 } from './stage3-rerank.js';
    36	import { executeStage4 } from './stage4-filter.js';
    37	import { MemoryError, withTimeout } from '../../errors/core.js';
    38	
    39	// Feature catalog: 4-stage pipeline architecture
    40	// Feature catalog: 4-stage pipeline refactor
    41	
    42	
    43	/** Per-stage timeout in milliseconds. */
    44	const STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000;
    45	
    46	/**
    47	 * Execute the 4-stage retrieval pipeline with per-stage error handling.
    48	 *
    49	 * Stage 1: Candidate Generation — MANDATORY (throws on failure)
    50	 * Stage 2: Fusion + Signal Integration — falls back to unsorted candidates
    51	 * Stage 3: Rerank + Aggregate — falls back to unranked scored results
    52	 * Stage 4: Filter + Annotate — falls back to unfiltered results
    53	 *
    54	 * @param config Pipeline configuration derived from search args
    55	 * @returns Pipeline result with stage metadata and timing
    56	 */
    57	export async function executePipeline(config: PipelineConfig): Promise<PipelineResult> {
    58	  const timing: Record<string, number> = {};
    59	  const pipelineStart = Date.now();
    60	  let degraded = false;
    61	
    62	  // -- Stage 1: Candidate Generation (MANDATORY — no fallback possible) --
    63	  let stage1Result: Stage1Output;
    64	  try {
    65	    const t0 = Date.now();
    66	    stage1Result = await withTimeout(
    67	      executeStage1({ config }),
    68	      STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS,
    69	      'Stage 1: Candidate Generation',
    70	    );
    71	    timing.stage1 = Date.now() - t0;
    72	  } catch (err) {
    73	    throw new MemoryError(
    74	      'PIPELINE_STAGE1_FAILED',
    75	      `Candidate generation failed: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`,
    76	      { cause: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err) },
    77	    );
    78	  }
    79	
    80	  // -- Stage 2: Fusion + Signal Integration (falls back to unsorted candidates) --
    81	  let stage2Result: Stage2Output;
    82	  try {
    83	    const t0 = Date.now();
    84	    stage2Result = await withTimeout(
    85	      executeStage2({
    86	        candidates: stage1Result.candidates,
    87	        config,
    88	        stage1Metadata: stage1Result.metadata,
    89	      }),
    90	      STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS,
    91	      'Stage 2: Fusion',
    92	    );
    93	    timing.stage2 = Date.now() - t0;
    94	  } catch (err) {
    95	    const msg = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);
    96	    console.warn(`[pipeline] Stage 2 failed, returning unscored candidates: ${msg}`);
    97	    degraded = true;
    98	    stage2Result = {
    99	      scored: stage1Result.candidates,
   100	      metadata: {
   101	        sessionBoostApplied: 'failed' as SignalStatus,
   102	        causalBoostApplied: 'failed' as SignalStatus,
   103	        intentWeightsApplied: 'failed' as SignalStatus,
   104	        artifactRoutingApplied: 'failed' as SignalStatus,
   105	        feedbackSignalsApplied: 'failed' as SignalStatus,
   106	        qualityFiltered: 0,
   107	        durationMs: 0,
   108	      },
   109	    };
   110	    timing.stage2 = 0;
   111	  }
   112	
   113	  // -- Stage 3: Rerank + Aggregate (falls back to unranked scored results) --
   114	  let stage3Result: Stage3Output;
   115	  try {
   116	    const t0 = Date.now();
   117	    stage3Result = await withTimeout(
   118	      executeStage3({
   119	        scored: stage2Result.scored,
   120	        config,
   121	      }),
   122	      STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS,
   123	      'Stage 3: Rerank',
   124	    );
   125	    timing.stage3 = Date.now() - t0;
   126	  } catch (err) {
   127	    const msg = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);
   128	    console.warn(`[pipeline] Stage 3 failed, returning unranked results: ${msg}`);
   129	    degraded = true;
   130	    stage3Result = {
   131	      reranked: stage2Result.scored,
   132	      metadata: {
   133	        rerankApplied: false,
   134	        chunkReassemblyStats: {
   135	          collapsedChunkHits: 0,
   136	          chunkParents: 0,
   137	          reassembled: 0,
   138	          fallback: 0,
   139	        },
   140	        durationMs: 0,
   141	      },
   142	    };
   143	    timing.stage3 = 0;
   144	  }
   145	
   146	  // -- Stage 4: Filter + Annotate (falls back to unfiltered results) --
   147	  let stage4Result: Stage4Output;
   148	  try {
   149	    const t0 = Date.now();
   150	    stage4Result = await withTimeout(
   151	      executeStage4({
   152	        results: stage3Result.reranked as Stage4ReadonlyRow[],
   153	        config,
   154	        stage1Metadata: { constitutionalInjected: stage1Result.metadata.constitutionalInjected },
   155	      }),
   156	      STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS,
   157	      'Stage 4: Filter',
   158	    );
   159	    timing.stage4 = Date.now() - t0;
   160	  } catch (err) {
   161	    const msg = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);
   162	    console.warn(`[pipeline] Stage 4 failed, returning unfiltered results: ${msg}`);
   163	    degraded = true;
   164	    stage4Result = {
   165	      final: stage3Result.reranked as Stage4ReadonlyRow[],
   166	      metadata: {
   167	        stateFiltered: 0,
   168	        constitutionalInjected: stage1Result.metadata.constitutionalInjected,
   169	        evidenceGapDetected: false,
   170	        durationMs: 0,
   171	      },
   172	      annotations: {
   173	        stateStats: {},
   174	        featureFlags: {},
   175	      },
   176	    };
   177	    timing.stage4 = 0;
   178	  }
   179	
   180	  timing.total = Date.now() - pipelineStart;

exec

    11	
    12	# CocoIndex Code Search Patterns
    13	
    14	Strategies for writing effective semantic queries and getting the best results from CocoIndex Code.
    15	
    16	---
    17	
    18	<!-- ANCHOR:overview -->
    19	## OVERVIEW
    20	
    21	Strategies and patterns for effective semantic code search using CocoIndex Code. Covers query writing, language and path filters, score interpretation, comparison with Grep, result verification workflows, and common query patterns by domain.
    22	
    23	---
    24	
    25	<!-- /ANCHOR:overview -->
    26	<!-- ANCHOR:writing-good-queries -->
    27	## 1. WRITING GOOD QUERIES
    28	
    29	Semantic search understands meaning, not just keywords. Write queries as you would describe what you are looking for to a colleague.
    30	
    31	### Recommended Query Ladder
    32	
    33	1. Start with a short concept phrase (3-5 words)
    34	2. Add a language filter when you know the language
    35	3. Add a path filter when you know the module
    36	4. Rephrase the concept only after filters are exhausted
    37	5. Switch to `Grep` for exact-text tasks
    38	
    39	### Use Natural Language
    40	
    41	| Good Query (semantic)                        | Bad Query (keyword-style)    |
    42	| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
    43	| "how does user authentication work"          | "auth"                       |
    44	| "error handling in API route handlers"       | "try catch"                  |
    45	| "database connection pooling setup"          | "pool"                       |
    46	| "file upload processing and validation"      | "upload"                     |
    47	| "rate limiting middleware implementation"     | "rate limit"                 |
    48	
    49	### Be Specific About Intent
    50	
    51	The more specific your query, the better the results.
    52	
    53	| Vague (many irrelevant results)         | Specific (targeted results)                           |
    54	| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
    55	| "config"                                | "database configuration with connection parameters"   |
    56	| "test"                                  | "unit test setup with mock dependencies"              |
    57	| "error"                                 | "error recovery when external API calls fail"         |
    58	| "middleware"                            | "authentication middleware that validates JWT tokens"  |
    59	
    60	### Describe Intent, Not Syntax
    61	
    62	Semantic search finds code by what it does, not how it looks.
    63	
    64	```
    65	Instead of: "async function"
    66	Write:      "asynchronous request handlers"
    67	
    68	Instead of: "for loop array"
    69	Write:      "iterating over collection items"
    70	
    71	Instead of: "if err != nil"
    72	Write:      "error checking in Go functions"
    73	```
    74	
    75	---
    76	
    77	<!-- /ANCHOR:writing-good-queries -->
    78	<!-- ANCHOR:using-language-filters -->
    79	## 2. USING LANGUAGE FILTERS
    80	
    81	Filter by language when you know which language you need results from. CocoIndex Code supports **28+ languages** (see tool_reference.md for the full list).
    82	
    83	### When to Filter
    84	
    85	- You are working in a specific language and want only relevant results
    86	- The codebase has multiple implementations of the same concept in different languages
    87	- You want to avoid noise from documentation or config files
    88	
    89	### Examples
    90	
    91	The `--lang` flag is **repeatable** -- specify it multiple times to filter by multiple languages.
    92	
    93	```bash
    94	# Find Python database models
    95	ccc search "database model definitions" --lang python
    96	
    97	# Find TypeScript React components
    98	ccc search "form validation component" --lang tsx
    99	
   100	# Find Go error handling patterns
   101	ccc search "error handling and recovery" --lang go
   102	
   103	# Find SQL migration scripts
   104	ccc search "table creation with foreign keys" --lang sql
   105	
   106	# Filter by multiple languages at once
   107	ccc search "authentication middleware" --lang python --lang typescript
   108	
   109	# Three languages
   110	ccc search "data serialization" --lang python --lang rust --lang go
   111	```
   112	
   113	**MCP equivalent:** The MCP `search` tool uses `languages` (a list of strings) instead of `--lang`:
   114	```json
   115	{
   116	  "query": "authentication middleware",
   117	  "languages": ["python", "typescript"]
   118	}
   119	```
   120	
   121	### When NOT to Filter
   122	
   123	- You want to understand a concept across the whole codebase
   124	- You are exploring unfamiliar code and do not know what language to expect
   125	- You want to find documentation alongside implementation code
   126	
   127	---
   128	
   129	<!-- /ANCHOR:using-language-filters -->
   130	<!-- ANCHOR:using-path-filters -->
   131	## 3. USING PATH FILTERS
   132	
   133	Scope searches to specific directories when you know where to look.
   134	
   135	### Examples
   136	
   137	```bash
   138	# Search only in API handlers
   139	ccc search "request validation" --path src/api/
   140	
   141	# Search only in tests
   142	ccc search "mock database setup" --path tests/
   143	
   144	# Search in a specific module
   145	ccc search "user permissions" --path src/auth/
   146	
   147	# Combine with language filter (--lang is repeatable)
   148	ccc search "error handling" --path src/services/ --lang typescript
   149	ccc search "error handling" --path src/services/ --lang typescript --lang python
   150	```
   151	
   152	### When to Use Path Filters
   153	
   154	- You know the feature lives in a specific directory
   155	- You want to avoid matches from unrelated parts of the codebase
   156	- You are investigating a specific module or package
   157	- For cross-CLI consistency: prefer explicit path filters over relying on the current working directory
   158	
   159	---
   160	
   161	<!-- /ANCHOR:using-path-filters -->
   162	<!-- ANCHOR:combining-filters-for-precision -->
   163	## 4. COMBINING FILTERS FOR PRECISION
   164	
   165	Combine query specificity, language filters, and path filters for the most targeted results.
   166	
   167	```bash
   168	# Highly targeted: TypeScript error handling in API layer
   169	ccc search "error handling with retry logic" --lang typescript --path src/api/ --limit 5
   170	
   171	# Find Python tests for database operations
   172	ccc search "database integration test fixtures" --lang python --path tests/
   173	
   174	# Find Rust memory management in core library
   175	ccc search "memory allocation and deallocation" --lang rust --path src/core/
   176	
   177	# Multi-language search scoped to a directory
   178	ccc search "configuration loading" --lang python --lang typescript --path src/config/
   179	```
   180	
   181	---
   182	
   183	<!-- /ANCHOR:combining-filters-for-precision -->
   184	<!-- ANCHOR:interpreting-relevance-scores -->
   185	## 5. INTERPRETING RELEVANCE SCORES
   186	
   187	Each result includes a relevance score from 0.0 to 1.0.
   188	
   189	| Score Range | Meaning                                           | Action                      |
   190	| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
   191	| 0.8 - 1.0  | Strong match: very likely what you are looking for | Read this first             |
   192	| 0.6 - 0.8  | Good match: probably relevant                     | Worth reviewing             |
   193	| 0.4 - 0.6  | Moderate match: somewhat related                  | Scan for usefulness         |
   194	| 0.0 - 0.4  | Weak match: tangentially related at best          | Usually skip                |
   195	
   196	**Tips:**
   197	- If top results score below 0.5, try rephrasing your query
   198	- If all results score above 0.8, your query is well-targeted
   199	- Scores are relative to the query, not absolute quality measures
   200

Read-only pass. Memory MCP calls were cancelled, so this is from local `rg` plus direct file reads.

The search system is split into four main surfaces:

- **`memory_context`** is the L1 orchestration layer. It classifies query intent, can route toward code-graph context, and delegates to `memory_search` or `memory_match_triggers` as needed. See [memory-context.ts](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/handlers/memory-context.ts:17).

- **`memory_search`** is the heavier indexed spec-memory search path. It now runs through a 4-stage pipeline: candidate generation, fusion, rerank/aggregate, then filter/annotate. Entry point: [memory-search.ts](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/handlers/memory-search.ts:15). Pipeline overview: [README.md](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/lib/search/pipeline/README.md:34).

- **`memory_match_triggers`** is the fast trigger-phrase path with cognitive/tier behavior: HOT gets full content, WARM gets summary, colder states are excluded. See [memory-triggers.ts](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/handlers/memory-triggers.ts:183).

- **CocoIndex + code graph** handle code search. CocoIndex is semantic search by meaning, exposed as an MCP `search` tool in [server.py](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/mcp_server/cocoindex_code/server.py:78). Code graph handles structural lookups and compact neighborhoods; `code_graph_context` accepts CocoIndex seeds too. See [context.ts](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/code_graph/handlers/context.ts:107).

Spec/doc anchors worth knowing:

- `/memory:search` documents the intended runtime: graph-first for structural queries, tri-channel retrieval, CocoIndex semantic channel, FTS5/BM25 fallback, adaptive fusion, MMR, reranking, and evidence-gap warnings. See [search.md](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/commands/memory/search.md:100).
- The 4-stage retrieval contract is documented in [pipeline/README.md](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/system-spec-kit/mcp_server/lib/search/pipeline/README.md:56).
- The major spec packet for indexing/adaptive fusion says the problem was stale CocoIndex paths, lazy code-graph init failures, and incomplete fusion trace visibility. See [spec.md](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/specs/system-spec-kit/023-hybrid-rag-fusion-refinement/011-indexing-and-adaptive-fusion/spec.md:53).
- CocoIndex query guidance lives in [search_patterns.md](/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.opencode/skills/mcp-coco-index/references/search_patterns.md:31).

My read: this repo treats “search” as a layered retrieval stack, not one tool. Memory search is for spec/history continuity, CocoIndex is for semantic code discovery, code graph is for structural code questions, and `memory_context` is the router that tries to keep those lanes from collapsing into one another.
